children.title: Can it take more work right now?
children.subtitle: Spare cores is the number to read. Above zero means there is room to start something. Zero means anything you start will queue behind what is already running.

children.value: State reads idle below 0.7 load per core, busy to 1.2, saturated to 2.0, overloaded above. Saturated is not broken — it means test gates and agents are already competing, so a new gate will run slow and may be killed by the machine rather than by your code.
Agents that wrote in the last 10 minutes

The tiles above read zero until the first Refresh — a zero before any refresh means no data yet, not an idle machine. Refresh reads the last snapshot the Mac pushed; it does not reach into the Mac itself. Ask Claude for a fresh reading; if Updated does not move, either no new snapshot has been taken since, or that refresh did not reach the server.

children.title: What did each prompt actually cost?
children.subtitle: Total written is the honest number: what the main session wrote plus what every agent it spawned wrote. Prompt length predicts almost nothing — the expensive ones are long back-and-forth builds, and a short question that fans out to many agents can join them.

children.value: Prompt length is the character count of what you typed — the point of showing it next to cost is that the two are barely related. Prompt text itself never leaves the Mac; the full ledger, with the text, stays in _claude/health/prompts.jsonl for reading there.

children.title: Is the machine getting more or less crowded?
children.subtitle: One reading per snapshot, oldest first, in the table below. Load climbing while agents stay flat means something heavy is running that is not an agent — usually test gates.

children.value: This is the light tail of the log — the last 240 readings. The complete history stays on the Mac in _claude/health/history.jsonl and is never uploaded, because it grows without limit and nothing here needs all of it.

children.title: A snapshot the Mac pushes, not a probe of the Mac
children.subtitle: This applet has no way to reach your machine. It reads one small file that your machine chose to publish.

children.value:
A Claude session on the Mac runs _claude/scripts/fleet-snapshot.sh. That script reads the machine's own counters (cores, load, running processes) and the Claude Code transcripts already on disk, then writes a snapshot locally and uploads a cleaned copy to https://167.233.64.97/fleet/snapshot.json.

This applet reads that one file. It holds no credentials and can change nothing — not on the server, not on the Mac.

The full efficiency log, the full per-prompt ledger, and every prompt's text stay local and are never uploaded.

What is uploaded carries no prompt text, no session identifiers, no file paths and no repository names — sessions and agents are numbered, not named. It is counts, timings and token totals — a few kilobytes.

The snapshot updates when a session on the Mac takes one — there is no background process and nothing on a timer. Updated on the Now screen is the moment of that reading, not the moment you tapped Refresh.

So the honest reading of a stale Updated is 'nobody has asked the Mac recently', not 'the Mac is quiet'.

Prompts queued is counted from queue events, and some of those events go missing when a session is interrupted or resumed. A session that has gone quiet is reset to zero, so an idle machine reads zero — but a session that is still active can carry a small overcount from earlier in its own run. Read it as a strong hint, not an exact depth.

Agent cost is attributed by timestamp: an agent's tokens go to whichever prompt was open when the agent wrote them. Spend that predates any known prompt boundary is set aside as unattributed rather than guessed onto a prompt.

Cost is shown in tokens written, not in money. Tokens read from cache are shown separately and are far cheaper per token — a prompt with a large cache-read number is not necessarily an expensive one.
